Deep in your brainstem, a tiny hub guesses what you'll feel before it happens.
It's the superior colliculus, six millimeters wide, long dismissed as a simple reflex relay for the eyes.
Regular MRI blurs it. So MIT and Mass General used a seven-tesla scanner with 1.1 millimeter voxels.
In animals, its layers split the jobs: shallow layers handle sight, deeper layers handle touch.
Eighty people confirmed it. Pictures lit the shallow layers. Pressure on the thumb lit the deep ones.
Then the twist. Before anything arrived, while people were just choosing a shape, those layers already lit up for what was coming.
A decoder trained on that pre-signal could tell which sense was coming.
Same screen, same button press. Only what they expected was different.
One caveat: the touch was unpleasant, so some of it may be preparation. Still, your oldest brain predicts.
